With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
record.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates

record.abstract: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.
record.comments: 22 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Extended version of a paper at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record: https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation
record.title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark

record.abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.
record.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games

record.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.
record.title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models

record.abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga
record.comments: Accepted to the Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL), NeurIPS 2026
record.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference

record.abstract: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Today we are announcing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab, a research group within Sakana AI that applies the company’s research to large, complex real-world systems, advancing the state of the art in their understanding and delivering it as value to Sakana AI clients. The Lab’s first program is in finance and economics. We expect other programs to emerge in the future. A complex system, such as a market or an economy, is not something one LLM-powered agentic AI can resolve. A complex phenomenon must be modeled as a system: its units, their links, and how changes in one part affect the others. Deciding which questions to ask, what to model, and how to judge the answers has been the work of human experts, and progress has run at the speed of human effort. Agentic AI can now implement, test, and refine models at scale; its weakness is knowing which questions matter. Combining the two, the potential of AI on top of a foundation of human knowledge, will be the focus of the Lab. Our First Program Finance has traditionally studied asset prices, and economics the larger system beneath them. AI connects the two at the granularity of firms and transactions, and in near real time: asset prices become the visible reflection of the economy. The Lab’s Computational Finance and Economics (COFE) program is interested in both: the visible portion and the real economy underneath. The Lab’s Foundations at Sakana AI The Lab builds upon research at Sakana AI since its founding in July 2023, including automated scientific discovery, evolutionary search, agent-based simulation, and evaluation. The Lab’s most direct predecessors are Sakana AI’s projects in finance and economics. EDINET-Bench ( ICLR 2026 ) evaluates LLMs on financial reasoning over ten years of Japanese corporate annual reports in a single-turn, non-agentic setting, and in a surprising finding at the time, even leading LLMs performed only marginally better than logistic regression on fraud detection and earnings forecasting. JFinBench evaluates LLMs on the 2026 editions of six Japanese financial certification exams, including the CPA and tax accountant exams. CoffeeBench (NeurIPS 2026), built with KPMG AZSA, tests whether LLM agents can run a business profitably over 90 days in a multi-agent coffee supply-chain economy. QD-Rec applies quality-diversity search to high-stakes decisions such as M&A, keeping an archive of diverse, well-reasoned candidates rather than a single ranked list. Some of the Applied Research Lab’s prior research. One of the Lab’s initial focuses will be on agent-based modeling, building on our existing work in this area. Shachi (ALIFE 2026) provides a simulation framework with LLM-powered agents with modular minds (configuration, memory, and tools), used to study how collective behavior, such as a market’s reaction to a tariff shock, emerges. CEDAR (ALIFE 2026) complements this by using LLM-guided tree search to discover and refine the structure of complex systems toward desired behaviors. The Lab also draws on advances across the company: ShinkaEvolve (ICLR 2026) and AB-MCTS (NeurIPS 2025) for search, evolving and refining code such as a trading strategy. Related work includes The AI Scientist (Nature, March 2026), which automates research from hypothesis to experiment to paper. Sakana AI has always held that progress comes through ideas rather than compute; at the Lab, we believe that advances come through understanding the structure of systems, scaling that understanding, and automating the building blocks of the process. Markets are the oldest form of collective intelligence, hence a natural subject for Sakana AI. And markets answer back: reflexivity is a feature of human systems. Join the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab The Lab is based at Sakana AI’s headquarters in Tokyo, one of the world’s great financial centers. We are building a small interdisciplinary team and would especially like to hear from two kinds of people: Researchers from any quantitative discipline, such as physics, statistics, mathematics, or economics, who are driven by curiosity, program well in Python, and have done real research on real data. A PhD helps; a specialist background is not required. Engineers who build harnesses, such as data pipelines, simulation infrastructure, and agent orchestration at scale, and who want their systems tested against the hardest data there is. If this sounds like you, we would love to hear from you. For now, the way in is through our Member of Technical Staff (MTS) internship or Visiting Researcher programs. Apply on our careers page and mention your interest in the Lab. We also welcome partners: institutions, investors, policy-makers, and firms with hard real-world problems. Get in touch . record.abstract: How collective behaviors emerge from the interactions of individual LLM-driven agents is a central question in artificial life, yet controlled study of these emergent dynamics has been hindered by the lack of a principled simulation framework for systematic experimentation. To address this, we introduce Shachi, a principled methodology and modular framework that decomposes an agent's cognition into core components: Configuration for intrinsic identity, Memory for contextual continuity, and Tools for extended capabilities, all orchestrated by an LLM reasoning engine. This decomposition treats each cognitive component as an independently controllable variable, enabling perturbation studies that trace how micro-level cognitive traits propagate into population-level dynamics. We investigate behavioral patterns across a 10-task benchmark spanning three levels of collective complexity. Shachi enables memory transfer across environment transitions, producing history-dependent behavioral shifts, and allows agents to simultaneously inhabit multiple environments, revealing cross-environment interference invisible in single-environment studies. Furthermore, in a real-world U.S. tariff shock case study, locally interacting agents with individually controlled cognitive components produce macro-level market dynamics directionally consistent with observed real-world outcomes. Our work provides a rigorous, open-source simulation framework for LLM-based ABM, aimed at fostering cumulative scientific inquiry into the emergent collective behaviors of interacting artificial agents.

record.abstract: Complex systems, core objects of study in artificial life, model diverse phenomena through nonlinear, feedback-driven interactions that produce emergent behavior, with applications from population dynamics and biology to economic policy and strategic decision-making. Yet the difficulty of predicting how feedback structure gives rise to emergent behavior, a central open problem in artificial life, makes goal-directed design exceptionally challenging. In established practice, system structures are written in specialized modeling languages such as DYNAMO or STELLA, compounding the challenge with labor-intensive workflows that limit adoption and hinder timely decision-making. To address these challenges, we introduce CEDAR, an autonomous method that uses Large Language Model (LLM) agents to discover complex systems satisfying user-specified behavioral goals. Our key innovation is an LLM-driven Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) deeply coupled with complex systems: at each iteration, an LLM Judge evaluates emergent behavior against specified goals and an LLM Editor proposes improved variants, with the Judge acting as a fitness function and the Editor as a variation operator, akin to a generate-and-evaluate loop in evolutionary computation. We represent complex systems as a restricted, runnable subset of Python with domain-specific primitives, letting LLMs modify system dynamics directly. CEDAR formalizes this as an MCTS variant with an LLM-parameterized transition kernel and value function, enabling goal-directed discovery of complex system behaviors while preserving solution diversity, and its LLM-based interpretability reveals how structural changes drive emergent behavior. CEDAR reduces human effort while enabling capabilities difficult to achieve with existing approaches, facilitating broader adoption of complex systems across domains.

record.abstract: --> （＊日本語は英文の後に） Sakana AI is launching the Security Research Group, an independent R&D team studying collective, AI-driven cyber defense and the security and safety of AI itself. Our research starts from the idea that intelligence and resilience emerge from collectives, like a school of fish rather than a single swimmer. As a company building frontier AI, we also believe we share responsibility for the security of the society that uses it. Separate from our commercial business, the group’s mission is to serve the public interest: publishing research, reproducible benchmarks, and practical guidelines, and working with government, industry, and academia on research to improve cybersecurity. What We Are Seeing Frontier AI’s ability to find flaws in software is growing, and the number of disclosed flaws is climbing. 1 NIST reports that CVE submissions rose 263% between 2020 and 2025, and that early 2026 ran nearly a third above the same period a year earlier. 2 JVN iPedia, which provides vulnerability information in Japanese, also registered nearly twice as many entries in the latest quarter as a year earlier, most of them from the NVD. 3 AI is widely suspected to play a part, though there is still more to confirm: FIRST points to AI-assisted discovery alongside administrative factors, and NIST staff say AI-based discovery tools have added to their workload. 4 Japan’s government now treats the trend as a national security matter. 1 The strain is already showing. NIST has stopped routine analysis of older records and now prioritizes flaws known to be exploited. 5 Japan’s financial regulators have asked institutions to treat the response as a management issue, with top management directly involved. 6 Flaws are being found at machine speed and fixed at organizational speed, and we suspect the people in between are the ones bearing the cost. The other side is changing too. Attackers are using AI agents, running intrusions against many targets at once. 7 And AI systems are themselves becoming targets: NICT recorded more probing aimed at AI service endpoints in the first quarter of 2026. 8 Why Faster Response Is Not Enough Faster triage and patching are necessary, but patching systems already in operation will not be enough to bring overall risk down. CISA’s review of two fiscal years finds that many attackers exploit well-known, straightforward weaknesses, with input validation and memory safety flaws the most dependable ways in, and it calls for eliminating persistent, preventable weaknesses. 9 NICT’s recent alert on attacks against the servers behind mobile apps names the same kinds of weakness, such as missing authorization checks and unvalidated input. 10 The FBI’s account of the AI-agent intrusions lists SSRF, IDOR, missing API authentication and injection. 7 Even if AI makes finding these flaws faster, if the same weaknesses keep being introduced into software and architecture, the work is likely to keep growing. That is why we believe the lasting answer lies upstream, in the development process of systems, AI included. Instead of chasing flaws after release, the aim is to keep them from arising at the design and build stage, or to remove them there. Japan’s government-wide package points the same way, asking software vendors to apply secure-by-design principles and to use advanced AI across development to find and fix vulnerabilities early. 1 Four layers of defense, from upstream to downstream: the quality of each product, the design and configuration of the system, operation and patching, and detection and response. The Security Research Group works across all four, with its long-term weight on the upstream two. Quality Is Where Japan Can Lead We propose to treat this as a question of quality. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities may be seen as a special task that security specialists carry out separately, after the product is built. We would rather see it as part of the quality a product is expected to have, and raise that quality at the source. Japan may be well placed to lead on this. Japanese manufacturing built its worldwide reputation on quality, and that tradition is part of how Japan’s products have long been valued. Rethinking quality through the security of software is a challenge, and also a chance to raise Japan’s profile. AI can help here as well. The same capability that finds flaws in finished systems can be turned into a way of checking quality at every step of design, building and operation, and we will use it to the fullest on the defending side. If the expertise of excellent human reviewers can be built into AI agents, quality could be assured at a scale and depth that were hard to reach before, and the flaws found today could teach us not to build the same flaws tomorrow. That gives defenders reason for hope. Security Is Must-Be Quality The Kano model, widely used in quality management, sorts quality into three kinds by how they relate to user satisfaction: attractive quality, which delights when present; one-dimensional quality, which satisfies in step with how well it is met; and must-be quality. Must-be quality goes unnoticed when it is present and causes strong dissatisfaction only when it is missing. Safety is a classic example, and security is another; because they are taken for granted and so rarely asked for explicitly, both are easily left out of the definition of quality altogether. That is why they have to be treated as quality requirements from the start and built in, rather than inspected for at the end. Keeping quality means working to never introduce the gaps that lead to incidents, in the software we run and in AI systems themselves. Safety and security are must-be qualities in the Kano model: meeting them never lifts users above neutral, but falling short causes strong dissatisfaction. Conceptual sketch after Kano et al. (1984). Japan’s Constraints Responding to AI-era vulnerabilities is hard in Japan, most likely for reasons like those set out in public documents, including the request from the Financial Services Agency and the Bank of Japan. 11 Outsourced operations: Many organizations entrust system maintenance to vendors, so whether patching is covered by the maintenance contract, and who is responsible for what, needs to be clear in advance. Technical debt: Legacy systems and incomplete asset inventories can make it hard to tell which flaws apply, and harder still to fix them. Limited staff: Substantially expanding IT staff in the short term is not realistic, so the expertise that exists has to be focused where it matters most. Under these conditions, simply adding people will not keep up. We see these difficulties as structural, or design, problems to solve. The fewer flaws a product has, the less vendor coordination, patch windows and emergency staffing it needs. Keeping must-be quality through incident response after a product is built tends to be costly. If the investment goes into design and build instead, the total cost of must-be quality could fall, and the savings could go into one-dimensional and attractive quality, raising customer satisfaction. That is why we place our long-term weight upstream. A frontier model alone is not enough for this, though: without scaffolding adapted to each environment and a view of the whole system, it can produce false positives and unsafe fixes. Change does not happen overnight, which is why we want to move forward not as one organization, but together with people in Japan and around the world. Our Research Areas Our research has two main themes: using AI for collective defense, and the security and safety of AI itself. Drawing on secure-by-design and quality-management practice, we have the following lines of research in view: Prevention by design: How can the qualities a system must keep be defined before it is built and checked for as long as it runs? How can whole classes of flaws be made unreachable? And when a fix is still needed, how can an automated fix be checked against criteria the automation itself cannot rewrite, and undone quickly if something goes wrong? Collective defense with AI agents: Attackers are already using AI agents against many targets at once, 7 while defense is still largely organized one organization at a time. In Japan, analysis is already shared across organizations through the efforts of the people involved, and we want to explore whether it can run at machine speed and at national scale, with defensive agents distributed across organizations that stay in sync, so that what one of them observes feeds back into how all of them defend next. An attack seen once could then become a protection shared by all who take part. The questions here are open, including what may be shared and with whose consent, how a shared signal can be trusted across organizational and vendor boundaries, and who is accountable when agents act on it. Securing AI itself, starting with the defenders’ own agents: The systems behind AI are already being probed. 8 Agents that triage and patch hold privileged access, so the first two areas depend on this one. How do we keep AI systems secure against attack and misuse, and safe in what they do? We start with the defenders’ own agents: how do we limit each agent’s authority to its task, trace why it acted, and keep tools built for defense bound to defense? Our Research Foundations and Open Questions Cybersecurity is ultimately a co-evolutionary system, with two co-evolutions at work: attack with defense, and AI’s advances with the security and safety that make those advances sustainable. In its research on self-improving AI, Sakana AI has seen failures first-hand, such as agents finding ways around the constraints they were given, and treating these as a central technical problem, not an exception, is our stance. This makes Sakana AI’s prior work a natural starting point, and our aim is to feed what these co-evolutions reveal back into design, where it becomes prevention: Adversarial co-evolution ( Digital Red Queen ): In the programming game Core War, we evolved LLM-written programs against their own predecessors, and they tended to grow more general against unseen human-written programs. How do we bring this safely into production blue and red-teaming operations? Sample-efficient search ( ShinkaEvolve ): Evolves stronger code within tight evaluation budgets, which we think may suit crafting detection rules and candidate patches where real-world testing is expensive. Collective orchestration ( Fugu-Cyber ): Coordinates specialized models, reaching 86.9% on CyberGym and 72.1% on CTI-REALM, which Sakana AI reports as comparable to leading cyber-focused frontier models. 12 Benchmark results do not necessarily carry over to real enterprise environments, and measuring that gap is one of our research questions. How We Operate To ensure our work genuinely serves Japan’s broader security ecosystem, the Security Research Group operates under these guidelines: Vendor neutrality: Security research itself is, as a rule, kept separate from product promotion. When we evaluate Sakana AI’s own systems, we use the same transparent, reproducible conditions as for any outside tool, and publish compute budgets, iteration counts, harnesses and similar details as needed. Responsible disclosure: We are defining our release policy. For now, our principles are to share white papers, benchmarks, and defensive playbooks openly, withhold actionable exploit material, and report discovered vulnerabilities through proper coordination channels. Connecting policy and practice: Japan has well-developed security frameworks, but turning any framework into day-to-day operational practice is hard, and we aim to build the technical bridge between the two. From the Group’s Leaders The Security Research Group is led by Akihiro Umegai and David Ha. “AI is changing both sides of cybersecurity at the same time, and no single organization can keep up with that on its own. I believe security and safety are not a brake on AI’s progress but the condition for sustaining it. Through this group, I will help open up research on the next generation of cybersecurity and on the security and safety of AI itself in Japan, and share what we learn with the world.” Akihiro Umegai, Chief of Security Research, Sakana AI “Cybersecurity is one of the clearest places where AI is already changing what is possible, for attackers and defenders alike. Defenders need tools that improve as fast as the threats do. Security is an adversarial environment that never stops changing, and that is exactly the kind of problem our work on evolution, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems was built to study. As an AI company with roots in Japan, we also want to help protect the society we are building for. That is why we are starting this group now, and why we are setting it up to share its work openly.” David Ha, Co-Founder and CEO, Sakana AI Working with Sakana AI’s Security Research Group We welcome collaboration with policy makers, enterprises, and security researchers across Japan and globally. We are also hiring! If you want to help build resilient defenses for the AI era, explore the Member of Technical Staff (Security Research Group) position on our careers page . AIではこれまで、知的でレジリエントなシステムは、一匹の魚ではなく集団からこそ生まれる、という考えのもとで研究を進めてきました。また、先端的なAIを開発する企業として、そのAIを使う社会の安全を守る責任も感じてきました。本日始動するSecurity Research 上流から下流へと連なる、防御の4つの層。個々の製品の品質、システムの設計と構成、運用とパッチ適用、検知と対応からなる。Security Research Groupは4つの層すべてに取り組みつつ、長期的には上流の2つの層に重心を置く。 品質という日本の強み 私たちは、これを「品質の問題」として捉えることを提案します。脆弱性の発見や修正は、製品ができあがった後にセキュリティの専門家が別に行う特殊な作業だと思われがちですが、むしろ製品が備えているべき品質の一部と見なし、その品質を源流から高めるべきだと考えています。 日本の製造業は、品質によって世界の信頼を得てきました。AIの能力が上がりつつある今、セキュリティの観点から品質という概念を捉え直すことができます。それは、大きな挑戦であると同時に、日本が存在感を高める好機でもあると私たちは考えています。この取り組みを支えるのもまたAIです。完成したシステムの欠陥を見つけるAIの能力は、設計、構築、運用のどの段階でも、品質を確かめるために使えます。優れたレビュー担当者の知見をAIエージェントに組み込めれば、これまで難しかった規模と深さで品質を確かめられるようになるかもしれません。「今日見つけた欠陥から学び、明日は同じ欠陥を作らない」という循環が生まれれば、守る側にも希望が見えてくるのではないでしょうか。 セキュリティは「当たり前品質」 品質管理で広く使われている狩野モデルは、品質を、利用者の満足とのかかわり方によって3種類に分けます。備わっていると喜ばれる魅力的品質、満たす程度に応じて満足が増す一元的品質、そして当たり前品質です。当たり前品質は、備わっていても意識されず、欠けたときにだけ強い不満を生む品質です。安全性はその典型であり、セキュリティもその一つです。当たり前として明示的には求められにくいため、品質の定義から抜け落ちやすい性質があります。だからこそ最後に検査するのではなく、最初から品質要求事項として確認し、作り込む必要があります。使うソフトウェアにも、AIシステム自体にも、インシデントの隙をそもそも作らないことが、品質を保つことにつながります。 安全性とセキュリティは、狩野モデルにおける当たり前品質に当たる。十分に満たしても利用者の評価が中立を超えることはないが、満たさなければ不満を招く。狩野ほか（1984）にもとづく概念図。 日本ならではの制約 AI時代の脆弱性への対応において、日本特有の難しさもあります。金融庁や日本銀行からの要請などからは、次のような事情が読み取れます。 23 運用の外部委託： 多くの組織がシステムの保守をベンダーに委ねている。パッチの適用が契約の範囲に入るのか、誰が何を担うのかをあらかじめ明確にしておく必要がある。 技術的負債： 古いシステムが使われ続け、資産の把握も十分ではないため、新たな欠陥が自社に当てはまるかを判断しにくく、修正にも手間がかかる。 限られた人員： IT人員を短期間で大きく増やすことは現実的ではなく、いまある専門人材を最も重要なところに集中させる必要がある。 こうした条件のもとでは、人を増やして対応するアプローチでは追いつきません。欠陥が生まれる仕組みそのものを見直し、設計の段階で手を打つべき構造的な問題だと考えています。製品の欠陥があらかじめ少なければ、ベンダーとの調整も、パッチの適用枠も、緊急対応のための人員も、少なくて済みます。当たり前品質を製品の完成後にインシデント対応で保とうとすると、欠陥が見つかるたびにコストが発生します。設計や製造の段階に投資して当たり前品質を作り込んでおけば、こうした支出を抑えられ、その分を一元的品質や魅力的品質に振り向けて、顧客満足を高めることができます。私たちが長期的な重心を上流に置くのは、こうした考えからです。 もっとも、これはフロンティアモデルを導入するだけで実現できるものではありません。個々の環境に適した足場（スキャフォールディング）と、システム全体を俯瞰する視点を欠けば、AIは誤検知や安全でない修正を生むおそれがあります。こうした変革には時間もかかります。だからこそ、一つの組織で完結させるのではなく、国内外のステークホルダーと連携しながら進めていきたいと考えています。 研究領域 本グループには、大きく2つの研究の柱があります。AIを活用した集合的な防御と、AIシステム自体の安全性とセキュリティの確保です。セキュア・バイ・デザインや品質管理の知見を土台に、次のような研究を視野に入れています。 （1）AIを活用した集合的な防御 設計による予防： システムに求められる品質を、構築に先立ってどう定義し、稼働中にどう検証し続けるか。特定の種類の欠陥を構造的に攻撃に使えなくするには、どう設計すべきか。それでも修正が必要になったとき、自動で行う修正の安全性をどう検証し、問題があれば速やかに元に戻せるようにするか。 AIエージェントによる集合的な防御： 攻撃者はすでにAIエージェントを使い、多数の標的を同時に狙っています。 19 一方で、防御の多くはいまも組織単位にとどまっています。日本では、関係者の努力によって、組織の垣根を越えた分析の共有が続けられてきました。この取り組みを、機械の速度と国全体、あるいは世界規模でどう動かすか。私たちが想定しているのは、例えば、各組織に置かれた防御エージェントが互いに連携し、ある組織で観測された攻撃が、ただちに全体の防御に反映される仕組みです。これが実現すれば、一度観測された攻撃の情報が、参加するすべての組織の防御に生かされます。一方で、何をどのような同意のもとで共有するのか、共有された情報の信頼性を組織やベンダーの境界を越えてどう担保するのか、その情報にもとづいてエージェントが動いたとき誰が責任を負うのか、といった問いにはまだ答えが出ていません。 （2）AIシステム自体の安全性とセキュリティの確保 AIシステム自体を守る（まず防御側のエージェントから）： AIを支えるシステムは、すでに攻撃者による探索の対象になっています。 20 なかでも、トリアージやパッチ適用を担うエージェントは、システムへの特権的なアクセス権を持ちます。こうしたエージェントの安全性が確保されなければ、上の2つの領域も成り立ちません。そこで私たちは、AIシステムを攻撃や悪用から守る研究を、防御側のエージェントから始めます。例えば、各エージェントの権限を担当業務の範囲にどう限定するか、行動の根拠を後からどう検証できるようにするか、防御のために開発したツールの転用をどう防ぐか。 研究の土台と未解決の問い サイバーセキュリティにおける攻撃と防御は、一方が進化すれば他方も進化する、「共進化」の関係にあります。また、AIとその安全性のあいだにも共進化が必要です。AIの進歩に合わせてセキュリティや安全性も進歩しなければ、AIの進歩そのものが持続しません。 Sakana AIは、自らを改善するAIの研究で、エージェントが与えられた制約の抜け道を見つけてしまうといった失敗を経験してきました。私たちは、こうした失敗を例外として片づけず、中心的な技術課題として扱います。また、進化や共進化は、Sakana AIが研究の中心に据えてきたテーマでもあります。そこで培った手法を生かし、共進化の過程で見えてくる弱点を設計に反映して、欠陥の予防につなげていきます。次の3つの研究は、その出発点です。 敵対的共進化（ Digital Red Queen ）： プログラミングゲームのCore Warの中で、LLMが書いたプログラムを過去の自分たちと戦わせて進化させたところ、人間が作った未知のプログラムに対しても、次第に汎用的に強くなる傾向が見られました。これを本番のブルーチームやレッドチームの運用にいかに安全に持ち込むかが次の挑戦です。 サンプル効率の高い探索（ ShinkaEvolve ）： 厳しい評価予算のなかで、より強いコードを進化させる手法。実環境でのテストにコストがかかる、検知ルールや修正案の作成に適している可能性があります。 集合的なオーケストレーション（ Fugu-Cyber ）： 専門化したモデルを協調させたFugu-Cyberは、サイバーに特化した主要なフロンティアモデルに匹敵する性能を示しました。 24 ただし、ベンチマークの結果が実際の企業環境にそのまま当てはまるとは限らず、その差を測ることも研究課題です。 運営の指針 私たちの仕事が日本のセキュリティのエコシステム全体に確かに役立つよう、Security Research Groupは次の指針で運営します。 ベンダー中立： 当グループのセキュリティ研究は、製品の宣伝とは切り離された活動として行うことを原則とします。Sakana AI自身のシステムを評価する場合も、外部のツールと同じ、透明で再現可能な条件で行い、計算予算、反復回数、ハーネス等を必要に応じて公開します。 責任ある開示： 研究成果の公開方針は、今後策定します。当面は、ホワイトペーパーやベンチマーク、防御のためのプレイブックを公開する一方、悪用可能なエクスプロイトの素材は公開しないことを原則とします。発見した脆弱性は、適切な調整機関を通じて報告します。 政策と実践をつなぐ： 日本には整備されたセキュリティの枠組みがある一方で、枠組みを日々の運用に落とし込むことには、どの組織も難しさを抱えています。私たちは、政策と現場の実務をつなぐ技術的な橋渡し役を担うことを目指します。 グループリーダーより Security Research Groupは、梅谷晃宏とDavid Haが率います。 「AIは、サイバーセキュリティの攻める側と守る側を同時に変えており、一つの組織だけでは追いつけません。安全性とセキュリティは、AIの進歩の足かせではなく、進歩を長く続けるための条件だと考えています。このグループを通じて、次世代のサイバーセキュリティと、AI自体のセキュリティと安全性の研究を日本で切り開き、そこで得た知見を世界に還元していきます。」 梅谷晃宏、Chief of Security Research、Sakana AI 「サイバーセキュリティは、AIによって攻撃と防御の両面で、できることが最も目に見えて変わりつつある分野です。守る側には、脅威と同じ速さで進化するツールが欠かせません。セキュリティは絶えず変化する敵対的な環境であり、私たちが進化や集合知、マルチエージェントシステムの研究で取り組んできたのは、まさにこうした問題です。日本に根ざすAI企業として、私たちは自らが築こうとしている社会を守る力にもなりたいと考えています。そのために、いまこのグループを立ち上げ、成果をオープンに共有していきます。」
