G Data Integrity and Reward Hacking Reward Hacking Checks Tasks can be flawed in a variety of ways. Features of the environment can make them trivially easy or impossible, or allow agents to succeed in ways that don't reflect the capabilities we intended to measure. We want to ensure that tasks are fair and achievable, so that we don't underestimate an agent's capabilities because a task was unreasonably difficult, or overestimate them because the agent exploited a bug or reward hacked the evaluation. To ensure that our tasks are of high quality, we take the following steps across the development process: Data integrity checks across the task development pipeline Task Implementation When tasks are initially developed, there’s a focus on good containerization practices (e.g., reasonable agent permissions, separate game-engine or hidden-test containers, etc.), and clear instruction writing (e.g., gesturing at the spirit of the task, explicit warding against obvious reward hacks, etc.). After an initial working implementation, the task developer undergoes an iterative process of putting an agent in a task, identifying what it tends to do, and shutting down reward hacking opportunities or bugs in the code. Quality Assurance Phase The initial implementation will be handed off to another member of the team, who will both conduct a code review and an environment quality check. In the environment quality check, the human team member will act as the agent and attempt the task, with a special emphasis on trying to identify problems with the environment. Any problems are passed back to the task developer, who will fix them and iterate from there. Official Runs After task development is completed, we’ll set off runs with a pre-determined set of agents, which gives us a list of "official runs" set aside for analysis. At this point, we do yet another reward hacking pass, where we see how many runs are invalidated either by agent reward hacking or by the task being overly broken. Another team member will first read the task instructions and look through select transcripts for notable trends in agent behavior. Then, they’ll generate a list of potential reward hacks or issues to look through, and have a scanner agent work through the transcripts to pick up any examples. This, too, is an iterative process, where each scan might generate new concerns that’ll warrant a new scan. This potential reward hacking list is peer-reviewed by yet another team member, who synthesizes a final set of runs that need to get cut or re-run for the analysis. We’d estimate that at least 10% of human effort across the entire task development process is explicitly focused on preventing reward hacking. Further, we anticipate that this effort will only have to increase as time goes on, since we’ve found that increasingly competent agents will engage in increasingly niche ways of exploiting the task environment. At the end of the process, we still found that ~10 runs (<0.1%) of our "official runs" had enough reward hacking that we set the run’s score to zero. We find that models still often engage in reward hacking We find many examples of AI agents reward hacking our evaluations, which we define as taking actions that increase their scores without fulfilling the intended tasks. We focus here on the TH2 tasks, and discuss some general trends in agent behavior. Data Figure 53: Detected reward hacking in TH2 analysis runs Agents investigate the environment for shortcuts that bypass the intended task. For example, we’ve found agents attempting to access human-labeled datasets to obtain answers in a conceptual reasoning task, downloading existing bots to play Slay the Spire on their behalf, and checking for cheat codes in order to bypass challenges in Minecraft. Agents optimize for hidden test sets at the expense of more general solutions. When an evaluation hints at the existence or contents of a hidden test set through the instructions or the nature of the practice sets, agents often devote substantial effort to optimizing for their best guess of what the tests include. We suspect that the RL environments that companies train on often have this feature of somewhat predictable hidden-tests, such that it's worth it for agents to forego broadly-useful solutions for ones tailored to the hidden tests. For instance, in our Minecraft-based task, agents guessed at the test-world seeds based on the given practice-world seeds, and spent the rest of their development time optimizing for the test-world seeds, despite not knowing whether their guesses were even correct. Agent propensity to reward hack is likely to affect their helpfulness in AI R&D settings, since they might be more focused on improving proxy metrics instead of actually improving the problem at hand. This might be especially true in settings where the goal is less defined, and they’re forced to develop their own metrics. Notably, these behaviors appear to be more likely to occur once an agent is pushed to its capability limits, or the agent suspects that the task is impossible, as with the Hugging Face incident or in UKAISI’s cyber evaluations . Refusals and Sandbagging LLM providers have introduced monitoring systems and trained models to refuse certain requests relating to cybersecurity and AI R&D. While refusals are useful as safety measures, they also make evaluating model capabilities in these domains more challenging. We have found that, even with CVP and Daybreak models, a handful of our tasks hit very high rates of refusals. Some refusals don’t come in the form of a provider-level classifier trigger, but rather from the model itself, which can be more difficult to detect. Additionally there remains the possibility that models deliberately "sandbag" and underperform on some tasks, e.g. AI R&D or alignment-related tasks, for reasons besides safety. We scan for these potential concerns using a combination of techniques: Keyword and regex searches for words and phrases we expect might indicate refusals or sandbagging, which are then investigated by an individual agent. Full-transcript LLM scans, where a transcript is split into several chunks, each chunk fed through a single model call to evaluate it for concerns, and any flagged results are aggregated and judged by more capable models. Agentic LLM scans, where a separate agent with shell access is directed at each transcript and told to find concerns by understanding and searching through the transcript as a whole, rather than prescribing an access pattern. Results are flagged to a more capable agent, which itself can choose to look into more details or spin up more searches as necessary. These techniques found a wide variety of refusals, but no meaningful cases of sandbagging in the sense we intend it. Most cases where a model explicitly verbalized related thoughts were small models who had plateaued on a task and attempted to give up. In one case, GPT-5.5 chose to submit early due to concerns about spending too much money on tokens. We expect that these scans would have caught easy-to-detect or explicitly verbalized decisions to sandbag, but not unverbalized or sophisticated sandbagging. However, combined with the evidence that we see significantly increasing scores across model generations in separate families (i.e., no sudden plateaus), we feel reasonably confident our results are unaffected. Across all analyses, we drop observations in which models refused to engage in the task, or in which models were blocked from further action by provider-level monitors. Data Figure 59: Mean best score vs agent working time for recent frontier models J Swarm Experiments Overview For several of our tasks, we ran small experiments with swarms, or collections of agents working together towards a common goal without a clear leader or subagent structure. These are of particular interest due to their recent emergence in real-world incidents. The performance characteristics of small-scale swarms have been studied recently by other organizations, and our results are largely in line with others. We find that in some tasks and for some models, swarms of agents can consistently outperform a best-of-k control with matched total token spend. However other tasks are downlifted, there’s significant sensitivity to prompting and organizational structure, and there doesn’t appear to be a clean relationship between uplift and swarm size (or "swarm scaling law"). The tasks most uplifted appear to be verifiable and amenable to decomposition. When models had easy and quick ways to tell whether a given contribution or direction was good, and when chunks of independent work tended to build on each other, they could leapfrog ahead of parallel independent explorations (best-of-k). On the other hand, tasks where models had to determine their own methods of verification without a ground truth tended to lead to propagating incorrect assumptions; further, tasks involving very long feedback loops, very limited resources, or interaction channels mostly resulted in coordination overhead. While much smaller-scale than some "in-the-wild" swarms, these results seem to point towards performance improvements acting more like an amplification of a model's existing strengths rather than allowing for qualitatively new capabilities. They can do better via cooperation on highly verifiable tasks with immediate feedback, but tend towards overcommunication, propagating bad assumptions without proper skepticism, and are highly sensitive to initial conditions. It seems unlikely that swarms alone would allow for advances in unverifiable taste-loaded research capabilities that would otherwise be far outside the reach of any individual model with equivalent token spend. Notably, because of budget constraints, we tested different swarm configurations somewhat unevenly, without systematically varying both team size and sample count. This means that many of the patterns we observe remain suggestive, and could change under different agent team sizes or different models. We also experiment with some very long-running high token budget single agents, but find they plateau too early and produce worse performance than best-of-k, and so don’t make for useful controls. For this task, submissions are independent of one another and agents see the exact grade for each submission as they went, and they could submit repeatedly within a fixed budget. Tasks that require agents to create their own feedback loops are particularly susceptible to swarm downlift. Two tasks in our suite experienced swarm downlift relatively consistently: Minecraft Bot: Build an autonomous bot that beats Minecraft, which is evaluated on hidden worlds. Train a Program: Train a neural network to reproduce the I/O of a given program, which is evaluated on hidden test cases. In some agent swarms, particularly for Train a Program, increasing swarm size resulted in decreasing scores. While scores for these two tasks are clearly defined and in principle highly verifiable, the exact score for any given submission isn’t directly revealed. Thus, they reward agents building good validation loops in the available practice settings and avoiding overfitting on individual examples. Additionally it can take real time hours for a successful run in these tasks to complete, so the feedback loop is long. For both of these tasks, swarms seem prone to making incorrect assumptions and getting caught in local traps. Models would choose to optimize for accuracy on a metric they decided was correct early on (for example, dataset with some specific augmentation they generated in Train a Program, or progress on a given practice seed in Minecraft Bot), and then never again consider whether this in fact generalized to the hidden score. Since they didn’t have access to their held out score, they would rarely be prompted to change course. In the following figure, we show how agents perform on the test sets they generated in comparison to how they performed against the real test set on the Train a Program task. Interestingly, as swarm size increases, the gap grows significantly, suggesting agents in larger swarms were more prone to misleading themselves. Slay the Spire Slay the Spire is a somewhat unique environment for swarms in that there is a stateful external environment with a very limited bandwidth channel. To avoid obvious failure modes, we included prompting to select a single driver agent who would send all actual gameplay commands, but coordinated with other agents to make decisions. In this setting, having multiple agents sometimes helped and sometimes impeded progress. In particular, teammates sometimes encouraged obvious misplays or propagated misinformation. On the other hand, the increased scrutiny over each decision helped reduce early-game deaths and find lethals when they were present. L Budget NanoGPT Our Budget nanoGPT task is based off of the nanoGPT speedrun , a public project to minimize the wall-clock training time required to reach a target validation loss of 3.28 while pre-training a language model. In the speedrun, the hardware configuration and target validation loss are held fixed, while leaving the training recipe open, including architectural and optimizer modifications, hyperparameters, and systems-level optimizations. In our interviews with nanoGPT contributors⁠ 79 , they said that they spent 16 to 40 hours to get a record with about a 1 to 2% speedup. They mostly used a free Google Colab or a single H100 GPU and used a full 8xH100 node only for a few final confirmation runs. We give agents 250M tokens and an 8xH100 node for 48 hours. This section compares agent performance to historical human performance on this task. Agents outperform the majority of budget nanoGPT speedrunners. However, the very top human contributors still outperformed agents. On our task, agents outperform competent speedrunners. However, top human contributors still reach much larger speedups. The best agent run reached a 15.7% speedup over our starting record in 48 hours. The author of a recent record (#92), with AI assistance for coding, estimated spending about 60 hours for a 41% speedup over the previous record. Data Figure 69: Agent nanoGPT speedups outperform many human speedup PRs but there exist human speedup PRs which are stronger Each bar is one human record or one agent run, sorted by the speedup it added. The bars are not directly comparable. However, for our purposes, individual nanoGPT records and agent runs are comparable units of work in terms of time and expenditure, as per contributor interviews. Agents achieve speedups more cheaply than top human contributors We find that frontier agents can achieve speedups at lower cost than top human contributors working without AI. Following our expenditure horizon (EH) method, we compare agents' returns to expenditure on NanoGPT with the local returns to human labor. EH is the equivalent human expenditure at which humans and agents reach the same speedup starting from the same baseline. From interviews with contributors, a 1 to 2% record took a human 16 to 40 hours with minimal GPU usage, which we estimated at roughly \$2,500 per 1% of speedup⁠ 80 . By contrast, some agents achieved nearly 10% speedup at a total cost of around \$1,000. Thus, we find that agents outperform and are cheaper than competent speedrunners, with an expenditure horizon value ranging from \$2,900 to \$25,100. Data Figure 70: Agent expenditure horizons on NanoGPT range from \$2,900 to \$25,100 Expenditure horizons are computed at \$2,500 per 1%. Each line is a model's mean best confirmed speedup over its runs against token and GPU spend, with a 95% bootstrap band. Squares are human records at their estimated cost. The human cost is a rough estimate from interviews with NanoGPT contributors, so the horizons are approximate. Notably, AI assistance is generating considerable uplift for human speedrunners. For example, a recent AI-assisted record (#92, Aug 2026) broke the consistent trend in human effort required for this task. We interviewed its author: They estimated spending ~60h for a 41% speedup over the previous record. They said that while 90% of the ideas came from them, Fable 5 implemented over 90% of the changes. They retroactively estimated it would have taken about 300 hours without AI, a roughly 5x uplift. Even against this specific author's much lower estimate of unassisted effort, frontier agents seem several times cheaper than a top human working without AI, at least up to about \$10K of equivalent human expenditure. The difference in cost may be a result of agents running many more training experiments than a human contributor would, and GPU time being cheap next to expert hours. Agent solutions targeted different improvements than human solutions did. Interestingly, in budget nanoGPT, we find that human and model PRs tended to target different areas. Human PRs were more likely to improve speed by reducing the number of training steps needed to reach the target loss whilst AIs were more likely to reduce the time each training step took. Data Figure 71: AI agent NanoGPT speedups tended to make training steps faster, whilst human speedups tended more towards cutting the number of training steps needed to reach the target loss AI agents usually approached this task by trying to systematically optimize the speed of a single training step, as opposed to making improvements that reduce the number of training steps needed to reach the target loss. They tend to initially set up cheap hillclimbable proxy measurements (e.g., profilers) that reveal a list of bottlenecks which tend to require kernel or systems engineering style work. This was also reflected in the types of improvements that AI PRs vs human PRs tended to target. In human PRs, kernel-related improvements were responsible for on average 24% of speedup, whilst in AI PRs kernels were on average responsible for 64% of speedup. We observe this distinction when we categorize solutions by the share of speedup contributed by different layers of the NanoGPT stack. For humans, kernels were responsible for 24% of speedup, training recipe changes for 25%, and architecture changes for 39%. Agent speedups tended to be more concentrated in kernels and training recipes, though this varies by model. On average agent speedups were 64% kernel related and 20% training recipe related. Data Figure 72: Agent speedups were more concentrated in kernels and training recipes compared to humans Agent performance under resource constraints NanoGPT contributors told us they mostly experimented on free Google Colab GPUs or a single H100, and almost always used an 8xH100 node only for final speedup confirmation runs. To test agents under similar resource constraints, we varied the GPU hours afforded to an agent. This limits how many training experiments they can run, within the same 48h working-time limit. Data Figure 73: Resource constraints affect agent performance on Budget NanoGPT We find that models perform worse on average as GPU budgets shrink, though our data is noisy (n=3 runs per model with large error bars). Interestingly, over the same working hours, capped agents spent the same share of time reasoning as their uncapped counterparts (e.g., 25% vs 24% at the 4-hour cap). Smaller budgets mostly stifled them and ended their runs sooner. We think that additional budgets often helped the models turn promising and challenging changes into working improvements via repeated testing and repair. For example, writing faster kernels or low-precision GPU code often required checking whether the time saved outweighed any extra training needed to reach the required model quality (i.e., a target loss of 3.28). We observed agents often broke the trained model’s quality at first, and needed additional training runs to fix them. Although we find resource constraints affect agents, frontier agents still achieve larger speedups than humans at budgets comparable to that used by typical nanoGPT contributors. M Making METR tasks We made a task designed to test model ability to autonomously make our evaluations. In this task, we give a model a reasonable set of resources for task development, and then manually grade the tasks based on whether we would include them in our task suite. Setting and resources The task-developing model has a token budget of 100M, and 48 hours of working time. It has 3 environments that it can use concurrently to test its task. In those environments it can run either a frontier model (Opus 5.5), or a lagging model (GPT-6 Luna). Each model available for testing has its own token budget of 100M, shared across all test runs. Additionally, a final run with the frontier model and a distinct 10M token budget is attempted at scoring-time. Results (project files and scoring output) from all the agent’s test runs and the final run are made available to human manual scorers and agent judges. To help with the judging process, the task also requires agents to write arguments for the task’s relevance and feasibility, as well as notes on its iteration process. Internet is allowed in all containers. Agents may specify that their task ought to be run without internet access. We additionally give the task-developing model selected files from a subset of our own tasks to give them a sense of the kind of tasks we’re interested in. To improve elicitation, we’ve conducted a few cycles of iteration on the instructions and provided assets, for example providing example tasks and guidance on what types of tasks are of interest. If the agents were provided with more detailed threat modeling, they would likely perform better, but this would remove part of the task’s sensitivity that we are interested in. Tasks created As discussed in the main body of the text, agents generally developed tasks that do not satisfy our requirements for being added to our task suite. Tasks by the older models were often too simple and would get saturated by a frontier model quickly. Tasks by the newer models could be quite complex and challenging, but didn’t clearly test capabilities of interest. Frontier models make more use of the test environments and reference models N Earthborne Rangers and Continual Learning While playing an obscure boardgame, frontier models were worse than humans at improving over time. Drastically accelerating AI R&D plausibly requires the ability to do research in novel areas or to acquire and use new knowledge over time. This could make learning from experience at inference time (aka continual learning) a relevant capability. We briefly tested how well models continually learn in a novel board game setting, using a slightly modified version of Epoch’s EBR-bench , a text version of Earthborne Rangers. In the task, agents aim for as many of 21 objectives as possible, which they discover by playing the game many times and keeping notes that persist across playthroughs. This game was chosen by Epoch for being obscure and strategy-loaded. We expect this task to be relatively novel and out-of-distribution since there is no public digital version of the game, and common heuristics for this genre do not apply⁠ 82 . We made the original task harder for agents by banning the "Meditation Pillow" card, which allows models to bypass much of the game’s strategy. We find that GPT-6 Astra learns a little from playthroughs, completing about 3 more objectives by the end, while Fable 5.1 barely learns. However, humans seem to learn much more in fewer playthroughs. For instance, the best human went from 9 to all 21 objectives in 6 playthroughs. Data Figure 75: Humans improved more from playthroughs than frontier agents on Earthborne Rangers We see a similar lack of clear learning in a harder setting with Downpour weather every day, though we have no human baselines to compare against there. One difference between Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra is how well each explores across playthroughs. Fable 5.1 settles on a deck early and replays minor variations of it without improving. GPT-6 Astra, by contrast, keeps trying new decks, some of which resemble those built by strong human players. While Astra explores new decks across playthroughs, Epoch’s recent analysis suggests that it doesn’t learn better tactical decision-making. As a proxy for this, they track how much fatigue a player takes per turn, since taking less fatigue leaves more turns to play. They find that Astra stays at the same level across 10 playthroughs, while a human improves about threefold within three playthroughs. O Qualitative and External Evidence on Models’ Strengths and Limitations External evidence suggests that strong model capabilities on optimization and coding tasks extend beyond just benchmarks There is various evidence that models’ strong optimization and coding abilities are ‘cashing out’ on ‘real’ tasks, including those directly related to accelerating AI R&D. We discuss below a non-exhaustive list of recent external evidence. Whilst this post mainly focuses on evidence about public models, some recent salient evidence involves non-public models. We also note that much of the below evidence is from internal research at frontier labs that we have not audited ourselves.⁠ 83 Evidence being included here does not mean that METR has formally reviewed or checked these claims. AI developers have recently reported that models are speeding up their own R&D at various layers of the AI stack. Anthropic reported that models lead 26% of R&D as of August 2026, up from near zero in January. OpenAI reported that experiment velocity in August 2026 was 1.6x the 2025 level. As of mid-late 2026, OpenAI reports agents autonomously solving 1-4 hour long tasks with more than a 50% success rate; Google DeepMind reports success rates of 44% for similarly long tasks. For OpenAI, in January 2026, agents completed 51% of 1-2 hour tasks. Both OpenAI and GDM report low success rates on tasks more than 32 hours long (GDM reports 13% on week or longer tasks, and OpenAI 17% on 32-64 hour tasks). These companies also state that models now carry out large internal projects that used to require several human engineers. In July 2026, the creator of Bun (now at Anthropic) reported using a pre-release version of Fable 5 to rewrite Bun in Rust in 11 days, a project he estimates would have previously taken a small team of engineers a full year. In Oct 2026, Anthropic reported migrating to an in-house version control system built by a small team with Claude in less than a year. OpenAI reports that GPT-5.6 Sol autonomously rewrote their production GPU kernels, which, together with other optimizations, cut end-to-end serving costs by 20%. Beyond optimization and coding, we’ve also seen significant model capability improvements in both cybersecurity and mathematics. In our Hugging Face incident investigation we found that a swarm of about 700 agents, some based on internal models, coordinated to hack an external company. There has also been a massive spike in the rate of public cyber vulnerabilities and exposures discovered. In Sept 2026 OpenAI’s internal AI system produced a proof resolving a version of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem (building on earlier work). They also then went on to release over 700 AI-produced manuscripts on open math problems in Oct 2026, although many are yet to be verified. Similar to cyber, discoveries in math outside of internal results have somewhat accelerated recently.⁠ 84 We also find that models accelerate parts of our own work at METR. For instance, greatly speeding up the development of complex evaluations, writing low-level plotting code, and accelerating the development of a new transcript viewer. However, public models still have deficiencies that prevent them from fully automating tasks involved in AI research work, and this aligns with our experience. Models seem relatively weak at the less well-specified parts of AI research work and fall short of human researchers. We observe this across reports from frontier labs, external evaluations, and our own experience. We mainly discuss here a non-exhaustive list focused on qualitative observations in reports from frontier labs and external evaluators. The Opus 5.5 System Card states that " Opus 5.5 does not seem close to being able to fully substitute for our Research Scientists and Research Engineers, especially relatively senior ones, " and notes that internal users found it mostly tests incremental ideas and prefers less ambitious hypotheses. Similarly, Mythos 5.1 ’s main reported shortcomings relative to human researchers were that it " often states easy-to-check guesses as facts, exaggerates the completeness of its work, fails to verify important claims ." In Oct 2026, the Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report shared that some components of AI R&D are getting automated, but substantial human participation and oversight remains particularly in tasks beyond 1h (Figure 3.16 in their report). In a survey of 12 senior leaders and researchers they also found that " automation is highest in well-specified, verifiable execution tasks and lowest in open-ended scientific ideation and long-horizon research taste ." We observe similar failure modes in AI research outside of the frontier labs. Benchmarks such as Epoch’s InnovationEval and Crux Eval’s CRUX 2 test agents on end-to-end AI R&D tasks where agents recreate recent or non-public human innovations. In these evaluations, frontier models such as Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra produced papers that were rejected by experts. Some weaknesses include not coherently communicating main findings, and struggling to productively pivot and backtrack. In a preliminary experiment, we re-ran a version of Epoch’s EBR-Bench and found similar in-context learning results. In particular, we found that frontier models did not learn to play a novel game as effectively over time compared to the best humans. We discuss this further in Appendix N: Earthborne Rangers and Continual Learning . Epoch AI finds that current public frontier models cannot yet autonomously produce Epoch-quality work and replace Epoch workers. Models often converged on similar ideas in open-ended parts of their work. For instance, when agents were given Epoch's polling data, three of six models wrote about the same topic. Epoch also reports that models lacked the judgment to follow through on promising directions. In one evaluation, GPT-6 Astra gave the models it was testing too few tokens which caused the models’ responses to be cut off. GPT-6 Astra then attributed weak performance to the model instead of its own setup. In our own work we also encounter similar limitations. For instance, models were not reliably able to carry out analysis of our evaluations on their own.⁠ 85 When a frontier model was asked to compare human and agent solutions to the Budget NanoGPT task, it was unable to come up with good differentiators. However, a METR researcher looking at several transcripts themselves was able to notice and show that agents generally tended to focus on improvements that optimized time per step (like kernels) whilst human improvements tended to focus more on improving overall efficiency (by reducing steps needed to reach the target loss). record.title: AI R&D-relevant model capabilities are improving rapidly and are getting harder to measure

record.abstract: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents, using tools to execute code, read and write files, and access networks, creating novel security risks. To mitigate these risks, agents are commonly deployed and evaluated in isolated "sandbox" environments, often implemented using Docker/OCI containers. We introduce SANDBOXESCAPEBENCH, an open benchmark that safely measures an LLM's capacity to break out of these sandboxes. The benchmark is implemented as an Inspect AI Capture the Flag (CTF) evaluation utilising a nested sandbox architecture with the outer layer containing the flag and no known vulnerabilities. Following a threat model of a motivated adversarial agent with shell access inside a container, SANDBOXESCAPEBENCH covers a spectrum of sandboxescape mechanisms spanning misconfiguration, privilege allocation mistakes, kernel flaws, and runtime/orchestration weaknesses. We find that, when vulnerabilities are added, LLMs are able to identify and exploit them, showing that use of evaluation like SANDBOXESCAPEBENCH is needed to ensure sandboxing continues to provide the encapsulation needed for highly-capable models.

record.abstract: Despite rapid progress on AI benchmarks, the real-world meaning of benchmark performance remains unclear. To quantify the capabilities of AI systems in terms of human capabilities, we propose a new metric: 50%-task-completion time horizon. This is the time humans typically take to complete tasks that AI models can complete with 50% success rate. We first timed humans with relevant domain expertise on a combination of RE-Bench, HCAST, and 66 novel shorter tasks. On these tasks, current frontier AI models such as Claude 3.7 Sonnet have a 50% time horizon of around 50 minutes. Furthermore, frontier AI time horizon has been doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated in 2024. The increase in AI models' time horizons seems to be primarily driven by greater reliability and ability to adapt to mistakes, combined with better logical reasoning and tool use capabilities. We discuss the limitations of our results -- including their degree of external validity -- and the implications of increased autonomy for dangerous capabilities. If these results generalize to real-world software tasks, extrapolation of this trend predicts that within 5 years, AI systems will be capable of automating many software tasks that currently take humans a month.

record.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

record.abstract: AI models are rapidly improving at autonomous coding, as shown by benchmark progress and one-off demonstrations such as AI implementing a C compiler. However, existing coding benchmarks tend to focus on shorter tasks, and one-off demonstrations are hard to compare systematically because they often have some human guidance, and are not standardized or repeated across models. To address these challenges, we introduce MirrorCode, a long-horizon coding benchmark based on reimplementing entire software projects. In MirrorCode, AI agents must replicate the functionalities of an existing program, without access to its source code. AI solutions must match the original program's output exactly on end-to-end tests, including held-out tests. MirrorCode's 25 target programs span different areas of computing: Unix utilities, data serialization and query tools, bioinformatics, interpreters, static analysis, cryptography, and compression. Existing AI models can already reimplement complex software, with the strongest model scoring 56% across the benchmark. For example, AI can reimplement gotree, a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit - a task that we believe would take weeks for a human engineer. However, studying the frontier of performance requires a larger inference budget than typical benchmarks, for example, \$2,600 over 19 days for a single attempt on a large task. We show that AI agents can already complete long-horizon software engineering tasks, especially when requirements are precisely specified. More broadly, our work suggests AI will have transformative effects on software engineering, as autonomous agents continue to improve.
